newsitem.title: MAURITIUS: Nigeria says export zones step to economic reform.
newsitem.headline: Nigeria says export zones step to economic reform.

text.p: Nigeria's Export Processing Zones (EPZ) is a key to overcoming the slow pace of the country's economic reform, Nigeria's High Commissioner to South Africa said on Tuesday.

High Commissioner Alhaji Shehu Malami told delegates to a sub-Saharan Oil and Minerals conference that in the past multi-national companies had been reluctant to make substantial investments in Africa due to concerns about infrastructure and endless bureaucracy.
But many African countries were now taking steps to reform their economies, including Nigeria.
"The reform process, however, takes time and is in no small measure dependent on the availability of resources.
"Consequently the establishment of export processing zones...have come to be seen as a means of overcoming such inadequacies," Malami said.
He said Nigeria's EPZ's was aimed at creating synergy in Africa's oil and gas sector.
In addition to an EPZ for export-orientated companies wanting to operate in the non-oil sector of Nigeria's economy, the country had set up the Onne/Ikpokiri Oil and Gas Free Zone.
"(It) is located strategically in the heart of the Gulf of Guinea where the most exciting oil exploration and production activity in the world is taking place," Malami said.
He said the huge potential of the Gulf of Guinea was being realised due to incentives provided by most countries in the region and technology that allows the development of deep water blocks.
"Current crude oil production in the sub-region is about 3.5 million barrels per day and is projected to rise to five million barrels per day by the year 2000.
"Similarly, natural gas production in the sub-region is set to expand in leaps and bounds from present production levels," Malami said.
He said multinational companies stood to gain from the EPZ.
"Oil and gas free zones are attractive for all operators in the petroleum industry".
